items.q: Discuss the perioperative management of an adult patient who underwent heart transplantation three years ago and now requires an appendicectomy.
items.model:
> **Verified examiner emphasis:** Assess graft function, altered physiology/drug responses, continue immunosuppression, include appendicectomy physiology and postoperative care; avoid distraction by an assumed pacemaker.

### Assessment and preparation
Treat appendicitis as urgent: assess sepsis, aspiration risk, hydration, electrolytes and renal function while contacting the transplant team. Establish graft function, exercise tolerance, recent echo/ECG, rejection episodes, cardiac allograft vasculopathy (CAV), arrhythmia, tricuspid regurgitation and any actual device. CAV may be silent; absence of angina is insufficient reassurance. New dysfunction or arrhythmia warrants targeted investigation without indiscriminate delay for routine tests.

Confirm all immunosuppressant names, doses and last administration. **Continue immunosuppression on schedule**, arranging an alternative route with the transplant service if nil by mouth; do not simply omit it. Check calcineurin-inhibitor concentrations when indicated, nephrotoxicity, K/Mg, marrow suppression, infection and drug interactions (including macrolides/azoles). Continue usual steroid; assess need for perioperative supplementation from dose, duration and surgical stress. Use asepsis and appropriate appendicitis antibiotics.

### Physiology and drugs
Denervation commonly produces a faster resting rate and attenuated immediate baroreflex responses; cardiac output responds to venous return and circulating catecholamines. Partial reinnervation is variable. Preserve adequate filling **without routine fluid loading**, especially with diastolic dysfunction, sepsis or renal impairment.

Direct catecholamines such as noradrenaline/adrenaline/isoprenaline remain effective and may produce marked responses; titrate. Ephedrine has mixed direct/indirect effects and is less predictable, not invariably ineffective. Atropine/glycopyrrolate chronotropy is unreliable; have direct chronotropy and pacing available. Adenosine sensitivity may be increased. Neostigmine-associated bradycardia has been reported despite denervation; use quantitative neuromuscular monitoring and an appropriate reversal plan.

### Anaesthesia and operation
If laparoscopic, pneumoperitoneum, positive pressure and head-up positioning can reduce venous return, while CO2 absorption and increased afterload add cardiac stress. Agree low insufflation pressure and immediate desufflation for unexplained instability. GA with a secured airway suits an urgent full-stomach patient; titrate induction to sepsis and graft reserve, prepare vasopressors, use ECG/SpO2/capnography/temperature and consider an arterial line if unstable or significantly impaired. Maintain oxygenation, normocapnia, perfusion, temperature and renal protection. Diagnose hypotension by cause rather than relying on reflex tachycardia or repeatedly giving fluid.

### Postoperative care
Choose monitored recovery/HDU/ICU according to graft dysfunction, sepsis and intraoperative events. Provide effective analgesia and ventilation, careful fluid/renal and rhythm review, timely immunosuppression and infection surveillance. Escalate new dysfunction for rejection/CAV assessment; give a named medication and transplant follow-up handover.
rubric: Assesses urgent abdominal/septic and aspiration risks alongside graft function/rejection/CAV
Explains denervation and variable reinnervation
Distinguishes reliable direct drugs from unpredictable antimuscarinic/mixed responses
Continues immunosuppression with route, interactions, renal and steroid plan
Explains pneumoperitoneum/ventilation effects and mitigation
Justifies technique, monitoring and haemodynamic treatment
Specifies postoperative level of care and transplant-team follow-through

items.q: You are asked to assess and anaesthetise a 54-year-old patient for a laparoscopic cholecystectomy. They received a heart transplant ten years ago. Discuss the issues relevant for this patient.
items.model:
> **Verified examiner emphasis:** Discuss denervation/drugs, immunosuppression and present graft function; explicitly address pneumoperitoneum.

### Establish current risk ten years after transplantation
Review original disease and transplant course, exercise tolerance, rejection, CAV surveillance, recent graft/valve and RV function, ECG/rhythm and any genuine pacing indication. Late CAV can be clinically silent; a long interval since transplant does not mean normal risk. New dyspnoea, dysfunction or arrhythmia needs transplant/cardiology assessment. Check renal impairment, hypertension, diabetes, infection/malignancy and medicine interactions; obtain targeted ECG, echo and laboratory tests rather than routine invasive investigations.

### Denervation and its practical consequences
Resting HR is often elevated and the immediate reflex response to low preload or vasodilation is blunted. Sympathetic/parasympathetic reinnervation is variable by ten years and cannot be assumed from elapsed time. Preserve venous return without overfilling. Silent ischaemia means haemodynamics, ECG and appropriate biomarkers matter more than angina alone.

Direct vasoactive drugs work: titrate noradrenaline for vasodilation and direct chronotropy/inotropy or pacing if required. Atropine is unreliable. Ephedrine is mixed acting, with variable effect. Adenosine may cause exaggerated block; neostigmine can cause bradycardia. Use quantitative blockade monitoring and a considered reversal plan.

### Laparoscopic cholecystectomy
CO2 insufflation can reduce venous return, increase SVR and cause hypercapnia; reverse Trendelenburg adds preload loss. These effects matter particularly when reflex compensation is impaired. Agree gradual low-pressure insufflation, careful position changes and desufflation if instability persists. Use a titrated GA with controlled ventilation, adequate analgesia and vasopressor availability. Add an arterial line for significant graft dysfunction or haemodynamic risk. Avoid hypoxaemia, major CO2 rise, hypothermia and prolonged hypotension; guide small fluid challenges by actual response.

### Immunosuppression and postoperative plan
Continue immunosuppressants without missed doses and arrange alternative administration if necessary. Check calcineurin nephrotoxicity, electrolytes, concentrations when indicated and antimicrobial interactions. Continue steroid and assess stress supplementation. Use asepsis, appropriate surgical antibiotics and renal-adjusted analgesia; avoid unnecessary nephrotoxins.

Plan monitored recovery and higher care for poor graft reserve or instability. Resume oral drugs on time, document fluid/renal/rhythm surveillance, infection review and responsibility for contacting the transplant service. Any new ventricular dysfunction or arrhythmia requires investigation rather than automatic attribution to anaesthesia.
rubric: Assesses present graft function, late rejection/CAV and comorbidities
Explains denervation with variable late reinnervation
Gives accurate direct/indirect/mixed and antimuscarinic drug responses
Explicitly addresses insufflation, hypercapnia and head-up position
Plans titrated anaesthesia, monitoring and cause-based support
Continues immunosuppression and covers renal/interactions/steroids
Gives a patient-specific postoperative monitoring and medication plan

items.q: Discuss how Marfan syndrome influences your anaesthetic management for a patient requiring an urgent laparoscopic appendicectomy.
items.model:
> **Verified examiner emphasis:** Prioritise cardiovascular BP control during laryngoscopy, pneumoperitoneum and emergence, airway and pulmonary/pneumothorax issues. Avoid exaggerated routine invasive/ICU plans or a generic septic full-stomach recipe.

### Key problem and assessment
Marfan syndrome is a connective-tissue disorder, commonly due to an FBN1 variant, with **aortic-root aneurysm/dissection, AR and mitral prolapse/MR** of greatest immediate cardiovascular concern. Assess usual surveillance imaging, aortic dimensions/growth, prior repair, valve function, symptoms and beta-blocker/ARB therapy. New abrupt chest/back pain, pulse/BP discrepancy, syncope or AR raises acute dissection: obtain urgent specialist imaging and change priorities. A current normal symptom history alone does not exclude aortic disease.

Urgent appendicitis adds sepsis, dehydration and aspiration risk. Review anticoagulation if prior mechanical valve and any pregnancy possibility. Obtain ECG and targeted echo/CT only for a management-changing question without unnecessary delay.

### Other systems that change anaesthesia
Look for difficult airway features (high-arched palate, crowded teeth, joint/cervical instability), chest deformity, scoliosis/restrictive physiology, bullae or prior spontaneous pneumothorax. Assess dural ectasia, spinal surgery and neurological symptoms if neuraxial analgesia is contemplated; dural ectasia can make spinal block unreliable and positioning difficult. Protect hypermobile joints, eyes and pressure areas.

### Conduct of anaesthesia
Use GA and a secured airway appropriate to the full-stomach/abdominal presentation. Plan airway technique and positioning from findings. Continue indicated rate/anti-impulse therapy unless haemodynamics contraindicate it; manage ARB according to indication and the agreed perioperative protocol. Avoid abrupt hypertension, tachycardia and marked contractility increases that raise aortic wall stress, while maintaining organ perfusion. An arterial line is reasonable with important aortopathy/valve disease or instability; choose access with known vascular anatomy in mind.

Pneumoperitoneum and head-up positioning can lower preload, increase afterload and CO2. Agree low pressure and gradual changes, maintain normocapnia and avoid excessive airway pressure, especially with bullae. Use titrated induction, analgesia and vasopressors rather than large abrupt cardiovascular changes. If significant AR coexists, **do not impose profound bradycardia blindly**: balance regurgitation/forward output with aortic protection with cardiology advice.

### Recovery
Smooth emergence, effective multimodal analgesia, respiratory and BP monitoring, surveillance for pneumothorax or dissection if new symptoms, careful antithrombotic restart and higher care according to aortic/valve severity. Ensure ongoing aortic surveillance and appropriate specialist follow-up.
rubric: Prioritises aortic/root dissection risk, AR/MR and previous repair/anticoagulation
Assesses current imaging and recognises symptoms requiring urgent aortic investigation
Covers airway, skeletal/dural, pulmonary and positioning issues
Accounts for urgent appendicitis, sepsis and aspiration
Explains laparoscopy/ventilation effects
Gives anti-impulse/perfusion goals while qualifying severe AR/bradycardia
Plans smooth emergence, monitoring and follow-up

items.q: A patient with type 2 diabetes mellitus requires urgent lower limb arterial bypass surgery. Their medications include dapagliflozin (a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor). Outline your specific concerns and management of this patient for this procedure
items.model:
> **Source/examiner emphasis:** Balance limb urgency against SGLT2 cessation/optimisation; explain euDKA diagnosis and treatment, cardiovascular/renal vasculopathy and specific glucose monitoring rather than vague targets.

### Establish urgency and current physiology
Clarify acute versus chronic critical limb ischaemia and the harm of delaying bypass; discuss timing with the vascular surgeon. Review dapagliflozin last dose, fasting/intake, diabetes treatment, HbA1c if available, infection, dehydration, renal function and systemic atherosclerosis (CAD, stroke, HF). Assess ECG/symptoms, Hb, electrolytes, renal function and vascular/bleeding/antiplatelet plans. Do not delay a threatened limb merely to complete an elective drug interval.

### SGLT2-specific risk
Dapagliflozin promotes glycosuria and relative insulin/glucagon imbalance; fasting, stress and poor intake can precipitate **ketoacidosis despite near-normal glucose**. Stop it now. Check capillary blood beta-hydroxybutyrate, glucose and a venous/arterial gas with bicarbonate, pH and anion gap. Significant ketonaemia with high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis supports euDKA; exclude lactate, renal and other causes rather than diagnosing it from glucose alone. Use the current local SGLT2 emergency algorithm; a rising ketone level or illness prompts urgent gas/specialist review even before severe acidosis.

If euDKA is present, seek endocrine/ICU help, give monitored fluid resuscitation tailored to HF/renal reserve, IV insulin **with glucose/dextrose to permit suppression of ketogenesis**, K replacement/monitoring and treatment of the precipitant. Continue until ketosis/acidosis resolves, not merely until glucose is normal. If safe, stabilise before anaesthesia; genuinely life-saving surgery may require simultaneous treatment.

### Intraoperative and postoperative plan
Use frequent glucose measurements, for example hourly during IV insulin/major unstable surgery, with a local target commonly around **6–10 mmol/L** and avoidance of hypoglycaemia. Repeat ketones/gas/electrolytes according to recent exposure, risk and trajectory. Supply carbohydrate/insulin appropriately and minimise avoidable fasting. Titrate anaesthesia, maintain coronary and limb/renal perfusion, use appropriate invasive monitoring and replace measured loss without overloading a failing heart.

Plan monitored postoperative care, renal and limb checks and written diabetes/antiplatelet instructions. Restart dapagliflozin only after acute illness resolves, adequate oral intake and absence of ketosis. For subsequent elective procedures, prescribe the actual local last-dose schedule; AHA/ACC/FDA uses ≥72 h for this drug, while ANZ calendar schedules are distinct and bowel preparation may require earlier cessation.
rubric: Balances threatened-limb urgency against metabolic optimisation
Assesses systemic cardiovascular/renal vasculopathy and medicines
Recognises euDKA despite normal glucose and checks ketones/gas/anion gap
Stops dapagliflozin and seeks endocrine/ICU advice for suspected ketoacidosis
Treats with fluid, insulin plus dextrose, potassium and precipitant control
Gives explicit glucose/ketone monitoring and a qualified target
Plans perfusion, higher care and safe restart/sick-day instructions

items.q: Justify your perioperative management of the following medications in a patient with type 2 diabetes mellitus scheduled for an elective laparotomy on a morning list: sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor (SGLT2 inhibitor); glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1 receptor agonist); once-daily subcutaneous long-acting insulin.
items.model:
> **Source/examiner emphasis:** Question paper only: no examiner report was available in the checked archive at the audit cutoff. No examiner emphasis, pass rate or official allocation is invented.

### Shared assessment
Confirm agents/formulations, usual timing, HbA1c/glucose, renal function, hypoglycaemia, intake and anticipated postoperative fasting. Give written last-dose, monitoring and restart instructions. A morning laparotomy can have prolonged fasting; coordinate diabetes/anaesthetic teams and minimise avoidable delay.

### SGLT2 inhibitor
Withhold before elective major surgery under an explicit current local schedule because fasting/stress can cause **euglycaemic ketoacidosis**. AHA/ACC/FDA uses ≥72 h for dapa/empa/cana and ≥96 h for ertugliflozin; ANZ calendar-day rules differ. For a prolonged low-carbohydrate diet or bowel preparation, cessation may need to precede that phase. Recent use or illness requires blood ketones and gas/anion-gap assessment; normal glucose is not reassuring. Suspected euDKA needs specialist fluid/insulin plus dextrose/K treatment. Restart only when stable with normal intake and no ketosis.

### GLP-1 receptor agonist
ANZCA/ADS/GESA/NACOS 2025 recommends **continuation**, rather than routine cessation, with a 24-h clear-fluid diet and the specified subsequent fasting plan. Delayed gastric emptying increases retained-content/aspiration risk; absence of GI symptoms does not reliably exclude it and stopping a long-acting agent briefly may not normalise emptying. If diet/preparation is incomplete, use the local risk-mitigation pathway: appropriately trained gastric ultrasound, selected prokinetic assessment, delay when appropriate or full-stomach airway precautions. The ANZCA April 2026 clarification specifies water only from six hours and no intake for the final two hours under that pathway. Tailor carbohydrate/insulin advice during the clear-fluid period and postoperative restart/continuation to tolerance.

### Once-daily long-acting insulin
Provide basal insulin at an **adjusted dose**, rather than automatically withholding all insulin. Many elective type-2 pathways use around **80% of the usual basal dose**, with the exact evening/morning schedule determined by formulation, usual administration time, renal function and hypoglycaemia risk. Confirm the institutional diabetes chart. For long fasting/major surgery or poor control, plan IV insulin with glucose and electrolyte monitoring; continuation of an adjusted basal dose during IV treatment depends on the protocol. Insulin is essential in type 1 diabetes; although this stem is type 2, do not generalise an omission rule across diabetes types.

Check glucose on admission and regularly, often hourly with IV insulin or unstable major surgery; a common target is approximately 6–10 mmol/L with local acceptable range. Treat hypoglycaemia promptly, monitor K, and prescribe postoperative transition to subcutaneous/enteral treatment with reliable food intake and no insulin gap.
rubric: Assesses formulation/timing, renal function, intake and glucose risks
Gives an exact SGLT2 hold strategy and accounts for bowel preparation
Detects euDKA by ketones/acidosis despite normal glucose and gives safe restart
Explains ANZ GLP-1 continuation plus diet/aspiration mitigation
Does not use absent GI symptoms as proof of an empty stomach
Adjusts basal insulin rather than automatic cessation and gives a protocol-based example
Plans glucose/K monitoring, IV insulin if needed and safe postoperative transition

items.q: A 68-year-old man is scheduled for total knee replacement next week. He has hypertension, for which he is prescribed enalapril, and type 2 diabetes, for which he is prescribed metformin. Justify your perioperative management of his medications.
items.model:
> **Verified examiner emphasis:** Justify stopping versus continuing each agent using physiology, patient risk and a coherent perioperative plan; a memorised drug list is insufficient.

### Patient and operation
Confirm BP control, HF/CAD, renal function, electrolytes, glucose/HbA1c, hypoglycaemia history and other medicines. Total knee replacement may involve neuraxial sympathectomy, bleeding, fasting and postoperative renal/volume changes. Plan prescribing and restart, not simply a preoperative omission.

### Enalapril
ACE inhibition treats hypertension and may treat HF, but reduces angiotensin-mediated compensation during anaesthesia; continuation increases hypotension risk. Conversely, omission can worsen BP control and interrupt useful HF treatment. STOP-or-NOT found similar major postoperative outcomes with continuation versus withholding, with more intraoperative hypotension after continuation.

Current policies differ: AHA/ACC allows withholding approximately 24 h in selected hypertensive patients having elevated-risk surgery and favours continuation for compensated reduced-EF HF; AoA/BIHS 2026 generally continues ACEI/ARB. **For this hypertension-only patient, document the local protocol and actual last dose**; withholding is reasonable if important hypotension/neuraxial or volume risk is anticipated, but is not universally mandatory. If continued, prepare for hypotension rather than cancel automatically. Treat hypotension by cause, with fluid for genuine deficit and titrated vasopressors; refractory ACE-related vasoplegia may require vasopressin. Restart once perfusion, renal function and potassium permit, with a named prescriber.

### Metformin
Metformin rarely causes hypoglycaemia alone. Accumulation with AKI or hypoperfusion increases lactic-acidosis concern. Confirm renal function, acute illness, expected fasting, route/intake and any contrast exposure. There is no mandatory 48-h preoperative cessation for every well patient.

For a short elective pathway with stable renal function, some current guidance allows continuation. For anticipated major surgery with prolonged fasting or AKI/hypoperfusion risk, withholding on the day is a reasonable local strategy. Explain the choice rather than claim one universal rule. Monitor capillary glucose at agreed intervals and treat hyperglycaemia with a defined insulin protocol if needed; metformin omission alone does not mandate an insulin infusion. Resume when eating, clinically stable and renal function remains appropriate; after AKI or relevant contrast exposure use the renal/contrast-specific reassessment pathway.

### Whole perioperative plan
Avoid dehydration and excessive fasting, maintain perfusion, monitor glucose and electrolytes, review renal function if clinically indicated and provide clear discharge instructions. Do not initiate a high-dose beta-blocker purely to compensate for withholding enalapril. Ensure the surgical/ward team knows which drugs were omitted and why.
rubric: Assesses indication, BP, renal function, electrolytes and glycaemic control
Weighs ACEI hypotension versus hypertension/HF treatment benefit
States the guideline difference and gives one coherent last-dose/monitor/restart plan
Explains metformin renal/hypoperfusion risk and low intrinsic hypoglycaemia risk
Avoids a universal 48-h metformin stop and gives a justified local plan
Plans glucose monitoring/rescue and renal-safe restart
Includes prescribing ownership and postoperative follow-through
